title_en: Clearing After Rain on Mount Inwang, by Jeong Seon
key_facts: Official title: 정선필 인왕제색도 (Jeong Seon's painting of Mount Inwang clearing after rain).|Painted by Gyeomjae Jeong Seon (1676-1759) in the Joseon dynasty.|On paper, 79.2 cm high and 138.2 cm wide.|Designated a National Treasure of Korea.

unverified_facts: Painted by Jeong Seon in 1751, late in his life.|Depicts Mount Inwang in Seoul as mist clears after rain.|A key work of 'true-view landscape' (jingyeong sansu): painting real Korean places rather than idealized Chinese scenes.|Dark, wet ink masses on the rock faces contrast with the pale mist.|Entered the National Museum of Korea through the Lee Kun-hee donation (2021).

title_en: Ssireum (Korean Wrestling), from the Album of Genre Paintings by Danwon
key_facts: One leaf of the album of genre paintings by Kim Hong-do (Danwon pungsokdo-cheop), designated a Treasure; 26.9 cm by 22.2 cm, on paper.|The museum calls it a masterpiece that represents the character of Kim Hong-do's genre painting.|Two groups of spectators sit in circles at the top and bottom, leaving an open space in the middle where two wrestlers grapple.|A taffy seller standing at the left is outside the crowd's attention but completes the circular composition; the shoes taken off narrow the empty space on the right.|Simple, quick brushstrokes capture the faces and the excited mood of the crowd; the rough lines match the cotton clothes, and the round faces and round eyes are typical of his genre figures.
source_note: e뮤지엄 작품 페이지의 기본정보·해설을 영어로 옮김. title_en은 작성자 번역

unverified_facts: An album of scenes of everyday life in late Joseon by Kim Hong-do.|Famous leaves include 'Ssireum' (Korean wrestling) and 'Village School'.|Figures are drawn with quick, lively brush lines and little or no background.|In 'Ssireum', spectators sit in a circle around two wrestlers.|Shows ordinary people working and playing, not only the elite.

title_en: Village School, from the Album of Genre Paintings by Danwon
key_facts: One leaf of the album of genre paintings by Kim Hong-do (Danwon pungsokdo-cheop), designated a Treasure; 26.9 cm by 22.2 cm, on paper.|The focus is a schoolboy crouching with his back turned, sobbing.|The other pupils sit in a circle around the teacher, who wears a scholar's square hat and Confucian robes.|The composition, the omitted background, and the brushwork of the clothes and faces give a lively, on-the-spot feeling.|The boy's sad face and the playful expressions of the people around him make viewers smile.

title_en: Portrait of Kang Se-hwang, painted by himself
key_facts: Official title: 강세황 초상 자필본, a portrait of Kang Se-hwang painted by Kang himself.|Kang Se-hwang lived from 1713 to 1791, in the Joseon dynasty.|On silk; 150.0 cm by 61.5 cm including the mounting.|Designated a Treasure of Korea.|The museum describes Kang Se-hwang as a leader of the 18th-century art world who learned Western painting methods via China and spread them, and who was also known as a calligrapher, writer, and official who served as governor of Hanseong (Seoul).|According to the museum, eight portraits of Kang Se-hwang survive.

unverified_facts: Kang Se-hwang painted himself at about age 70 (1782).|He wears an official's black gauze hat together with informal scholar's robes, an unusual combination.|His own inscription explains the combination: his mind is in the mountains and forests while his name is on the court roster.|Kang was a scholar-painter and art critic, and a teacher of Kim Hong-do.

title_en: Endless Rivers and Mountains, by Yi In-mun
key_facts: Painted by Yi In-mun, a court painter of late Joseon whom the museum ranks alongside Kim Hong-do; he was good at landscapes, figures, and grapes rather than true-view landscapes or genre scenes.|On silk, 43.9 cm high and 856 cm long; designated a Treasure.|The museum calls it an unprecedented large work in Korean painting history: five pieces of silk were joined to depict an endless ideal landscape.|People living in harmony with unchanging nature appear throughout; tiny, finely drawn figures and varied, ornate texture strokes for the mountains create a dramatic view wherever the eye moves.|Yi In-mun reorganized the landscape as if looking down from a high place far away.|Seals reading 'Chusa' and 'Chusa jinjang' show that it once belonged to Kim Jeong-hui (1786-1856).

title_en: Painting of the Rhapsody on the Sound of Autumn, by Kim Hong-do
key_facts: Official title: 김홍도 필 추성부도, by Kim Hong-do (1745-1806?), Joseon dynasty.|On paper, 214.7 cm by 55.8 cm; designated a Treasure.|The inscription on the painting is the text of the 'Rhapsody on the Sound of Autumn' (Chuseongbu), whose narrator is Master Ouyang (Guyangja).|In the text, Master Ouyang, reading at night, hears a sound coming from the southwest and sends his servant boy to look; the boy says the stars and moon are bright and the sound is in the trees.|The narrator sighs that it is the sound of autumn; at the end the boy nods off, and only the chirping of insects is heard around the walls.

title_en: Woman Carrying a Baby on Her Back, by Shin Yun-bok
key_facts: Painted by Shin Yun-bok (1758?-after 1817), known for genre paintings of the romantic feelings of young men and women.|On paper, 23.3 cm by 24.8 cm.|A woman carrying a baby on her back is painted on a small sheet with no background.|At the lower right he wrote his pen name 'Hyewon' and stamped a square seal reading 'Wa-gan-un'.|The tall, slender young woman with a wide skirt and a large wig looks like a gisaeng (female entertainer), and the baby on her back conveys motherly love.|A long inscription by an unidentified writer, 'Buseol Geosa', compares the picture with paintings of beautiful women by the Tang Chinese painter Zhou Fang and notes that Zhou's paintings had no child on the back.

title_en: Mother Dog and Puppies, by Yi Am
key_facts: Painted by Yi Am (1499-?), a great-grandson of Grand Prince Imyeong; little is known of his life, but he is said to have excelled at painting animals.|According to the Veritable Records of King Injong, he was recommended together with Yi Sang-jwa to paint the portrait of King Jungjong.|His animal paintings show an independent style with a Korean feeling; here the mother dog and puppies are painted in a warm mood.|The dogs are painted in some detail, with the changes of fur color softly blurred, while the tree in the background is simplified.|On paper, 163 cm by 55.5 cm.

title_en: Plants and Insects, attributed to Shin Saimdang
key_facts: Attributed to Shin Saimdang (1504-1551), the mother of the scholar Yi I and a leading woman painter of early Joseon; she excelled at poetry, calligraphy, painting, and embroidery.|This is one of the plants-and-insects paintings from an eight-panel screen; on paper, 32.8 cm by 28.0 cm.|The watermelon, mice, and butterflies show delicate lines, bright colors, and a stable composition.|Many plants-and-insects paintings are traditionally attributed to Shin Saimdang, and later they were often used as models for embroidery.
